before.content_html:
Why Bonding Determines Properties

The physical properties of a substance — its melting point, hardness, electrical conductivity and whether it dissolves in water — all depend on its type of bonding and structure. This is one of the most powerful ideas in chemistry: if you know how the atoms are held together, you can predict how the material will behave. Examiners regularly test this link, so every property you state must be explained in terms of the forces involved.

Metallic Bonding

In a metal, atoms are arranged closely together in a giant metallic structure. The metal atoms lose their outer electrons, leaving a lattice of positively charged metal ions surrounded by a ‘sea’ of delocalised electrons. Strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the negative electrons holds the whole structure together.

This model explains several key properties. Metals conduct electricity because the delocalised electrons can drift along the structure when a voltage is applied. They conduct heat well because those same mobile electrons transfer kinetic energy quickly. Metals are malleable and ductile — the layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking, because the delocalised electrons can reorganise to maintain attraction throughout. High melting and boiling points arise from the strength of the metal–electron attraction.

Key Fact

Metallic properties explained: conducts electricity (delocalised electrons carry charge), malleable (ions slide over each other), high melting point (strong attraction between ions and electron sea).

Giant Ionic Structures

Ionic compounds such as sodium chloride form a giant ionic lattice. Many strong electrostatic forces act in all directions between the positive and negative ions. This gives ionic compounds high melting and boiling points because a great deal of energy is needed to break all these forces.

Ionic compounds do not conduct electricity when solid because the ions are locked in fixed positions. When melted or dissolved in water, the ions become free to move and carry charge — so they conduct electricity in these states. Most ionic compounds dissolve in water because water molecules can surround and pull away individual ions from the lattice. Ionic solids are often brittle: applying force shifts layers, so like charges align and repel, shattering the crystal.

Key Fact

Ionic compounds: high melting points (many strong electrostatic forces), conduct when molten or dissolved (ions free to move), do not conduct as solids (ions fixed in the lattice). A common exam error is saying solid ionic compounds ‘have no ions’ — they do; the ions just cannot move.

Simple Molecular Substances

Simple molecular substances (such as water, carbon dioxide and methane) have strong covalent bonds within each molecule but weak intermolecular forces between molecules. When the substance melts or boils, it is the weak intermolecular forces that are broken — not the covalent bonds. This means simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points and are often liquids or gases at room temperature.

Simple molecular substances do not conduct electricity in any state because they have no free electrons or ions. A very common exam mistake is to say the covalent bonds are weak — the bonds within the molecules are strong; it is the forces between molecules that are weak.

Larger molecules have more electrons and so form stronger intermolecular forces. This means they need more energy to overcome those forces and boil. For example, methane (\ (CH_4\)) has a much lower boiling point than octane (\ (C_8H_{18}\)) even though both are alkanes with similar covalent bonds within each molecule. The difference in boiling point reflects the difference in intermolecular force strength, not bond strength within the molecule.

Giant Covalent Structures

Giant covalent structures contain billions of atoms bonded together by strong covalent bonds in a continuous network. They have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken. Carbon forms several giant covalent allotropes.

Carbon can form four covalent bonds. In diamond, each carbon bonds to four others in a rigid tetrahedral arrangement, making diamond extremely hard and a non-conductor (no free electrons — all four bonding electrons are used in covalent bonds). In graphite, each carbon bonds to three others in flat hexagonal layers; one electron per carbon atom is delocalised within each layer, so graphite conducts electricity. The layers are held together by weak forces, allowing them to slide, making graphite soft and slippery. Graphene is a single layer of graphite — one atom thick, very strong, and an excellent conductor with potential uses in electronics and composite materials.

Silicon dioxide (found in sand and quartz) is another giant covalent structure. Like diamond, it has very high melting and boiling points and does not conduct electricity. Each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms in a network that extends in all directions.

before.content_html:
The Reactivity Series

Metals can be placed in order of how readily they form positive ions. The more easily a metal loses its outer electrons, the more reactive it is. Chemists have arranged metals in a reactivity series, with potassium, sodium, lithium and calcium at the top, then magnesium, aluminium, zinc and iron in the middle, and copper, silver and gold at the bottom. Carbon and hydrogen are included as non-metal reference points — their positions determine how metals can be extracted and which metals react with dilute acids.

The order from most to least reactive is: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, hydrogen, copper, silver, gold. The reactivity of a metal is related to how easily it forms its positive ion — metals higher in the series lose electrons more readily because their outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electron shells.

Key Fact

A metal’s position in the reactivity series determines how it reacts with water and dilute acids, whether it can displace other metals, and which extraction method is used. The higher the metal, the more easily it loses electrons to form positive ions.

Reactions with Water and Dilute Acid

Very reactive metals (potassium, sodium, calcium) react vigorously with cold water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. For example, sodium reacts rapidly: \(2Na(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + H_2(g)\). Calcium reacts more gently, producing a cloudy solution as calcium hydroxide has limited solubility.

Moderately reactive metals (magnesium, zinc, iron) react slowly or not at all with cold water but react well with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen gas. For example: \(Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow MgCl_2(aq) + H_2(g)\). Copper, silver and gold are below hydrogen in the reactivity series and do not react with dilute acids at all, because they do not lose their electrons readily enough.

Displacement Reactions

A displacement reaction occurs when a more reactive metal replaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt. The more reactive metal loses electrons more readily and ‘pushes out’ the less reactive metal, which is deposited as a solid.

A classic example is iron placed in copper sulfate solution. Iron is above copper in the reactivity series, so it displaces copper:

$$Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)$$

The blue solution turns pale green (iron(II) sulfate) and a brown copper deposit forms on the iron. No reaction occurs if a less reactive metal is placed in a solution of a more reactive metal’s salt — for example, copper will not displace iron from iron sulfate solution.

You can determine a reactivity order by systematic displacement experiments. Place different metals into solutions of other metals’ salts and observe whether a displacement occurs (colour change, a solid deposited, or a temperature rise). If displacement occurs, the added metal is more reactive. By testing several combinations, you can rank the metals in order. You can also compare how vigorously metals fizz with dilute acid — faster bubbling and greater heat released indicates higher reactivity. This kind of evidence-gathering is the practical foundation of the reactivity series.

Extracting Metals from Their Ores

The method used to extract a metal depends on its position in the reactivity series. Metals below carbon in the series can be extracted by reduction with carbon. The carbon is more reactive, so it displaces the metal from its oxide. In this redox reaction, the metal oxide is reduced (loses oxygen) and the carbon is oxidised (gains oxygen). For example, extracting zinc from zinc oxide:

$$2ZnO(s) + C(s) \rightarrow 2Zn(l) + CO_2(g)$$

Metals above carbon in the reactivity series (such as aluminium, sodium and potassium) cannot be extracted by carbon because they are too reactive — carbon cannot pull the oxygen away from them. Instead, these metals must be extracted by electrolysis, which uses electrical energy and is therefore more expensive. The need to use a finite non-renewable ore and large amounts of energy makes metal extraction an important sustainability issue.

Scientists are developing biological alternatives for extracting metals from low-grade ores. Phytoextraction uses plants to absorb metal compounds through their roots; the plants are harvested and burned, and the metal is recovered from the ash. Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce acidic leachate that dissolves metal compounds from the ore; the metal is then recovered by displacement or electrolysis. These methods are slower than conventional extraction but can work on ores that would otherwise be waste, reduce energy costs, and lower the amount of toxic metals left in landfill. Deciding whether to use them involves weighing these benefits against the slow production rate (IaS4 — risk–benefit reasoning under practical constraints).

Key Fact

Metals below carbon in the reactivity series are extracted by reduction with carbon (a cheaper process). Metals above carbon are extracted by electrolysis (more expensive — uses large amounts of electricity). The position of carbon in the series is the key to explaining the extraction choice.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The reactivity series ranks metals by how readily they form positive ions; more reactive metals displace less reactive ones from solutions of their salts.
  • Metals below carbon in the series are extracted by reduction with carbon; metals above carbon are extracted by the more expensive process of electrolysis.
  • Biological extraction methods (phytoextraction and bioleaching) offer lower-energy alternatives for low-grade ores, but they are slower — a trade-off that requires careful evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Explain, in terms of electrons, why magnesium is more reactive than copper.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: magnesium loses its outer electrons more easily than copper; this is because magnesium’s outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are held less strongly; the easier the electron loss, the more reactive the metal. Secure: magnesium loses electrons more easily, correct reference to electron shells. Developing: magnesium is higher in reactivity series with some attempt at electron reason. Emerging: magnesium is more reactive without explanation.

before.content_html:
What Is Electrolysis?

Electrolysis is the process of using an electric current to break down an ionic compound. The compound must be in a state where its ions are free to move — either molten (heated until liquid) or dissolved in water. Solid ionic compounds cannot be electrolysed because the ions are held in fixed positions within the lattice and cannot carry the current.

The ionic compound used in electrolysis is called the electrolyte. It is placed in a container called an electrolytic cell, and two electrodes are connected to a power supply. The electrode connected to the positive terminal of the supply is the anode, and the electrode connected to the negative terminal is the cathode.

Key Fact

Anode = positive electrode (oxidation occurs). Cathode = negative electrode (reduction occurs). Positive ions (cations) move to the cathode; negative ions (anions) move to the anode.

What Happens at the Electrodes

At the cathode, positive ions (cations) arrive and gain electrons. This is reduction. Metal ions are reduced to metal atoms; hydrogen ions are reduced to hydrogen gas. At the anode, negative ions (anions) arrive and lose electrons. This is oxidation. The products depend on what ions are present.

Half equations show what happens at each electrode separately. For example, in the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride:

$$\text{At cathode: } Na^+(l) + e^- \rightarrow Na(l) \text{ (reduction)}$$

$$\text{At anode: } 2Cl^-(l) \rightarrow Cl_2(g) + 2e^- \text{ (oxidation)}$$

So electrolysis of molten sodium chloride produces sodium metal at the cathode and chlorine gas at the anode. For molten binary compounds (two elements only), prediction is straightforward: the metal or hydrogen forms at the cathode; the non-metal forms at the anode.

When an ionic compound is dissolved in water, the water itself also contains \(H^+\) and \(OH^-\) ions. This creates competition at each electrode. At the cathode, either the metal ion or hydrogen ion from water is reduced, depending on relative reactivity. If the metal is less reactive than hydrogen (e.g. copper), copper is deposited at the cathode. If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen (e.g. sodium), hydrogen gas is produced instead because the water’s \(H^+\) ions are discharged more easily than sodium ions. At the anode, either oxygen is produced (from \(OH^-\) ions in water) or the halogen is produced if a concentrated solution of halide ions is present. For example, electrolysis of aqueous copper sulfate with inert carbon electrodes gives copper at the cathode and oxygen at the anode; electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution gives hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode.

Extracting Aluminium by Electrolysis

Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the Earth’s crust but is too reactive to be extracted using carbon reduction. Instead, it is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (from the ore bauxite). The aluminium oxide must be heated to a very high temperature to melt it, which uses a large amount of energy and makes the process expensive.

In the cell, aluminium ions are reduced at the cathode to form liquid aluminium metal, which sinks to the bottom and is tapped off. At the anode (made of carbon), oxygen ions are oxidised to form oxygen molecules. The oxygen reacts with the carbon electrodes at this high temperature, forming carbon dioxide and gradually burning away the electrodes — so the carbon anodes must be replaced regularly. This adds to the overall cost of production.

Question: What are the products of electrolysing aqueous copper(II) sulfate solution with inert (carbon) electrodes?
Step 1 — Identify all ions present: Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻ from the salt; H⁺ and OH⁻ from water.
Step 2 — Cathode (reduction): Cu²⁺ or H⁺ will be reduced. Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so Cu²⁺ ions are discharged in preference to H⁺. Product: copper metal deposited on the cathode.
Step 3 — Anode (oxidation): SO₄²⁻ or OH⁻ will be oxidised. No concentrated halide ions present, so OH⁻ is oxidised. Product: oxygen gas released at the anode.
Half equation at cathode: \(Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu(s)\)
Half equation at anode: \(4OH^-(aq) \rightarrow 2H_2O(l) + O_2(g) + 4e^-\)

Key Fact

In the electrolysis of aqueous solutions: metals less reactive than hydrogen are deposited at the cathode; metals more reactive than hydrogen produce hydrogen gas instead. At the anode, oxygen is produced unless a concentrated halide solution is used, in which case the halogen (e.g. chlorine) is produced.

practice_questions.text: Name the electrode at which oxidation occurs during electrolysis.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: anode. Developing: cathode. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to a cation when it reaches the cathode during electrolysis.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the cation gains electrons at the cathode and is reduced to a neutral atom or molecule. Secure: gains electrons and becomes neutral. Developing: becomes a neutral atom. Emerging: moves to cathode.

practice_questions.text: Explain why copper is deposited at the cathode rather than hydrogen gas being produced when aqueous copper sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: both Cu²⁺ and H⁺ ions from water are present at the cathode; copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so Cu²⁺ ions are more easily discharged than H⁺; therefore copper metal is deposited in preference to hydrogen. Secure: copper below hydrogen in reactivity series, so copper discharged first. Developing: copper is less reactive. Emerging: copper goes to cathode.

practice_questions.text: Compare the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride with the electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride solution. Explain how the products at the cathode differ and why.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: molten NaCl — only Na⁺ and Cl⁻ present, so sodium metal produced at cathode; aqueous NaCl — Na⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺ and OH⁻ present; sodium is above hydrogen in reactivity series so H⁺ ions are discharged in preference, producing hydrogen gas. Secure: identifies difference (Na vs H₂) and gives reactivity reason. Developing: names different products. Emerging: gives product for one condition only.

practice_questions.text: Aluminium is one of the most widely used metals in the world, yet its production by electrolysis is very expensive. Evaluate the factors that contribute to the high cost of aluminium production, and suggest why we should still invest in recycling aluminium rather than extracting it from ore.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: factors (aluminium above carbon so electrolysis required; high temperature to melt aluminium oxide; large electricity input; carbon electrodes burn away and must be replaced); recycling arguments (uses far less energy than extraction from ore; conserves finite bauxite reserves; reduces environmental impact of mining; economically viable despite collection costs). Secure: three cost factors identified and two recycling advantages with explanation. Developing: two factors identified, recycling mentioned. Emerging: electrolysis is expensive, recycling is better — without reasons.

practice_questions.text: Write the half equation for the reaction at the cathode when molten lead bromide (PbBr₂) is electrolysed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: \(Pb^{2+}(l) + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb(l)\) — correctly balanced charge and atoms, reduction identified. Secure: correct formula, correct electrons, minor error. Developing: direction of electrons correct but equation unbalanced. Emerging: identifies lead at cathode without equation.

lessons.title: Crude Oil and the Hydrocarbon Industry

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a feedstock in the chemical industry.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a raw material used as the starting point for making other chemical products. Secure: raw material for making other chemicals. Developing: starting material. Emerging: vague reference to industry.

practice_questions.text: Describe how crude oil is separated by fractional distillation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: crude oil is heated so it vaporises; the vapours rise up a fractionating column that is cooler at the top; different fractions condense at different heights depending on their boiling points and are collected. Secure: heated, different boiling points, condense at different heights. Developing: mentions boiling points. Emerging: heated and separated.

practice_questions.text: Explain why petrol, which has shorter hydrocarbon chains, condenses near the top of the fractionating column while bitumen remains as a liquid residue at the bottom.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: shorter chains have weaker intermolecular forces; less energy is needed to overcome them, so they have lower boiling points and remain as vapour higher up the cooler column, condensing near the top; bitumen has very long chains with much stronger intermolecular forces and a much higher boiling point, so it never fully vaporises and remains as residue at the base. Secure: shorter chains, weaker forces, lower boiling point — all three linked. Developing: shorter chains have lower boiling point. Emerging: shorter molecules go to the top.

practice_questions.text: A chemist cracks dodecane (C₁₂H₂₆) and obtains ethene (C₂H₄) as one product. Suggest what the other product is and write a balanced equation for the reaction.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: other product = decane (C₁₀H₂₂); balanced equation: \(C_{12}H_{26} \rightarrow C_{10}H_{22} + C_2H_4\); identifies decane as an alkane and ethene as an alkene. Secure: correct formula for both products, equation balanced. Developing: identifies products but equation unbalanced. Emerging: names one product.

practice_questions.text: Crude oil is used in huge quantities worldwide both as a fuel and as a chemical feedstock. Evaluate the sustainability of our current dependence on crude oil, and suggest what chemists can do to address the problems it creates.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies crude oil as finite; current consumption rate not sustainable; consequences (depletion, price rises, loss of feedstock for future polymers/medicines); for fuels — development of renewable alternatives (hydrogen, biofuels, electric vehicles); for feedstock — development of bio-based polymers and recycling of existing polymers; role of increased atom economy; societal cost–benefit decision (IaS4 framing). Secure: finite nature identified, two future alternatives with explanation, sustainability conclusion. Developing: finite nature and one alternative. Emerging: mentions crude oil running out.

practice_questions.text: Explain what cracking is and why it is economically important for the petrochemical industry.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: cracking breaks down long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful molecules using heat and a catalyst or steam; it is economically important because demand for shorter-chain fuels (petrol) and alkenes (for polymers) is greater than supply from distillation alone, so cracking converts surplus heavier fractions into higher-value products. Secure: defines cracking and gives one economic reason. Developing: describes cracking process. Emerging: cracking splits molecules.

lessons.title: Material Choices and Life Cycle Assessment

practice_questions.text: Name two physical properties that would be important when choosing a material for a frying pan handle.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: any two from: low thermal conductivity (so it does not get hot); high melting point or does not soften at high temperature; hard/rigid/stiff (stays in shape under force). Award 1 mark for any one correct property. Developing: names a property without relevance to the context. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a life cycle assessment (LCA).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: an analysis that evaluates the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life, from raw material extraction to disposal. Secure: covers all stages of product life, assessing environmental impact. Developing: considers environmental impact of a product. Emerging: looking at how eco-friendly something is.

practice_questions.text: Explain why reusing a product has a lower environmental impact than recycling it.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: reusing extends the life of the product without any reprocessing, so no energy is needed for collection, sorting, melting or reforming; recycling requires collection, transport, sorting and reprocessing, all of which use energy and may produce waste or emissions; therefore reuse avoids these energy costs entirely. Secure: reuse needs no energy for processing, recycling does — two clear points. Developing: reuse is better for the environment with one reason. Emerging: reusing saves materials.

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer is deciding whether to make a sports drinks bottle from glass or PET plastic. Compare the properties and LCA considerations of each material and suggest which would be more suitable. Justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: glass is heavier, higher density (less suitable for sports use), does not leach chemicals, high melting point so can be sterilised, but is brittle and heavier; PET is lighter (important for portability), tough, transparent, can be recycled; LCA: glass can be reused many times and recycled; PET uses crude oil feedstock (finite) but is lightweight (less transport energy); justified conclusion relating to the sports context (likely PET for lightweight, shatterproof use). Secure: two relevant property comparisons, one LCA point, reasoned conclusion. Developing: compares one property. Emerging: names one material without comparison.

practice_questions.text: A recycling company claims that making a cotton tote bag has a lower environmental impact than making a plastic carrier bag. A journalist argues the opposite, citing a government LCA report. Evaluate which source is likely to be more reliable and explain what an LCA would need to include to settle the argument.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: recycling company has a financial interest in promoting the cotton bag so may cherry-pick data; government LCA report is more likely to be independent and peer reviewed but may still be limited by data availability; to settle the argument the LCA needs to include: all four stages (extraction, manufacture, use and disposal) for both products; energy use, water use, greenhouse gas emissions and biodegradability at each stage; typical number of uses per bag; disposal route (landfill, incineration, recycling, composting); the cotton bag uses more water in cotton farming and more energy in manufacture, but is biodegradable; the plastic bag uses less water and energy in manufacture but is non-biodegradable and is derived from a finite resource; conclusion must acknowledge subjectivity and note that the answer depends on usage pattern and disposal. Secure: identifies bias in company data; names three LCA components; one comparison between bag types. Developing: identifies one source as more reliable with one reason; names two LCA stages. Emerging: mentions LCA without critical evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Suggest why PET drinks bottles can be economically recycled, but some other plastic products cannot.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: PET bottles are produced in very large quantities so are abundant in the waste stream; they are easy to identify and sort; the market for recycled PET (fibres, new bottles) is well established; some other plastics are produced in smaller quantities, are harder to sort (mixed compositions), or have little market for recycled material — making collection and processing economically unviable. Secure: abundance in waste stream, ease of sorting, and/or established market. Developing: PET is common and has a use. Emerging: vague.

knowledge_checks.q: What is a life cycle assessment (LCA) used to evaluate?
options: The cost of manufacturing a product
The total environmental impact of a product across all stages of its life
The physical properties of a material
The number of times a product can be recycled

knowledge_checks.q: Why can LCAs be partly subjective?
options: They only consider the manufacturing stage
Different analysts may weight different environmental impacts differently and data may be incomplete
They are always funded by governments
They do not include disposal stage impacts

lessons.title: Bonding, Structure and Why Properties Differ

practice_questions.text: State why diamond is harder than graphite.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: in diamond each carbon forms four covalent bonds in a rigid network; in graphite only three bonds hold each carbon in layers that can slide. Award 1 mark for any answer stating that diamond has more/stronger bonds or a 3D network. Developing: mentions bonds but is vague. Emerging: diamond is harder.

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of a thermosetting polymer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: long polymer chains joined to each other by covalent cross-links forming a rigid three-dimensional network; these cannot be broken by heating without destroying the polymer. Secure: cross-linked polymer chains, does not soften on heating. Developing: has cross-links. Emerging: cannot be melted.

practice_questions.text: Explain why graphite is used as a lubricant.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: graphite has a layered structure; each carbon forms three covalent bonds, creating flat hexagonal layers; the forces between the layers are weak so the layers can slide easily over each other, allowing surfaces to move with less friction. Secure: layers held by weak forces, can slide easily — two linked points. Developing: mentions layers sliding. Emerging: graphite is slippery.

practice_questions.text: Compare thermosoftening and thermosetting polymers in terms of their structures, properties and suitability for recycling.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: thermosoftening — chains held by weak intermolecular forces, soften on heating, can be reshaped and remoulded, recyclable by melting; thermosetting — chains cross-linked by covalent bonds, do not soften on heating, cannot be remoulded, not recyclable by melting. Secure: correct structure and property for each type, recycling difference noted. Developing: one type described accurately. Emerging: one property for each.

practice_questions.text: A materials engineer is developing a new sports helmet. The helmet must be rigid and not deform under impact, must be lightweight, must not conduct electricity, and must maintain its shape at temperatures up to 150°C. Evaluate whether a thermosoftening polymer or a thermosetting polymer is more suitable, justifying your answer with reference to structure and bonding.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: thermosetting polymer is more suitable; covalent cross-links form a rigid three-dimensional network — this explains rigidity under impact; cross-links also prevent softening at 150°C (thermosoftening polymers would soften at this temperature as their weak intermolecular forces are overcome); polymers are generally lower density than metals so the lightweight requirement is met; polymers are electrical insulators (no free electrons) so the conductivity requirement is met; disadvantage: thermosetting cannot be recycled by melting, which has an environmental cost. Conclusion: thermosetting is more suitable for all the stated requirements despite the recycling drawback. Secure: correct identification, three linked structure–property arguments, reasoned conclusion. Developing: correct identification with two property arguments. Emerging: identifies thermosetting without structural justification.

practice_questions.text: Explain why graphene has potential uses in electronics and as a strengthening additive in composites.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms in a hexagonal arrangement; one electron per carbon is delocalised making it an excellent electrical conductor — useful in electronics; every bond in the sheet would need to be broken to tear it, giving extraordinarily high tensile strength — useful for strengthening composites. Secure: conductivity from delocalised electrons and high strength from covalent network. Developing: mentions conductivity or strength with one structural reason. Emerging: graphene is useful in electronics and composites.

knowledge_checks.q: Why can thermosetting polymers not be recycled by melting?
options: Their chains are cross-linked by covalent bonds that cannot be broken by heating
They are made from crude oil
Their intermolecular forces are very weak

knowledge_checks.q: How many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form in graphite?
Graphite conducts electricity because each carbon forms only three bonds, leaving one electron per carbon _____ and free to carry charge.
Thermosoftening polymers soften when heated because the chains are held together by weak _____ forces that can be overcome at moderate temperatures.
Match each carbon allotrope to its distinguishing structural feature:
right: Single atom-thick layer of hexagonal carbon
Four bonds per carbon, 3D tetrahedral network
Layered hexagonal structure with delocalised electrons between layers

before.content_html:
What Makes a Nanoparticle?

A nanoparticle is a particle with at least one dimension between 1 and 100 nanometres. To put this in context, a single nanometre is one-billionth of a metre — a human hair is roughly 80,000 nm wide. Nanoparticles sit between individual atoms (which are typically 0.1–0.5 nm across) and bulk materials that we handle at everyday scales. This “in-between” scale is what makes them scientifically interesting and commercially valuable.

The key feature of nanoparticles is their extraordinary surface-area-to-volume ratio. When you divide a lump of material into many tiny nanoparticles, the total surface area increases enormously while the total mass stays the same. More surface area means more atoms are at the surface and available to interact with other substances — reactions and interactions that occur at surfaces happen far more readily than in the bulk of a material.

Key Fact

Nanoparticles have a very high surface-area-to-volume ratio compared with the same material in bulk form. This increases reactivity and changes other properties such as colour, strength, electrical conductivity and melting point.

Properties That Change at the Nanoscale

Many materials behave differently at the nanoscale from their bulk counterparts. Gold is a classic example: in bulk form it is shiny and yellow, but gold nanoparticles can appear red or purple depending on their size because their electrons interact with light differently. Graphene is another example — a single layer of carbon atoms only 0.3 nm thick, yet stronger than steel and an excellent electrical conductor. These emergent properties are not simply predictable from the bulk material’s properties; they arise from quantum effects and the dominance of surface atoms.

Other properties that can change at the nanoscale include:

• Melting point — nanoparticles often melt at lower temperatures than the bulk material because surface atoms are less tightly bound.
• Electrical and thermal conductivity — some materials become better conductors or better insulators at the nanoscale.
• Colour — the wavelengths of light absorbed and reflected change with particle size.
• Catalytic activity — increased surface area makes nanoparticles far more reactive as catalysts, allowing reactions to proceed faster at lower temperatures.

Uses of Nanoparticles

The unusual properties of nanoparticles make them useful across a wide range of applications. You need to be able to evaluate these uses alongside the associated risks — this is a classic risk–benefit analysis that science cannot answer alone.

Traditional sunscreens used large particles of titanium dioxide or zinc oxide, which left a thick white residue on the skin. By reducing these particles to the nanoscale, manufacturers created sunscreens that are transparent while still absorbing and scattering ultraviolet radiation effectively. The high surface-area-to-volume ratio of nano-sized titanium dioxide means more UV radiation is absorbed per gram of material, allowing effective protection with a much thinner layer.

The benefit is clear: a wearable, cosmetically acceptable product that encourages people to apply sun protection and thereby reduces skin cancer risk. The uncertainty is whether nanoparticles can penetrate damaged or sunburnt skin and enter cells. If they did, the high reactivity that makes them useful could potentially be harmful inside living tissue. Research is ongoing, and regulatory bodies have reviewed the evidence several times; current scientific opinion is that the particles are unlikely to penetrate intact healthy skin in meaningful quantities, but the question is not fully settled.

Other established uses of nanoparticles include:

• Medicines and drug delivery: nanoparticles can carry drugs directly to target cells (such as cancer cells), reducing side effects on healthy tissue. Some silver nanoparticles are incorporated into wound dressings and medical equipment because silver ions are toxic to bacteria but generally safe for human cells at low concentrations.
• Self-cleaning glass: titanium dioxide nanoparticles on window glass react with UV light to break down organic dirt, which is then washed away by rain. This property is called photocatalysis.
• Electronics: computer chips and memory devices use nanotechnology to pack more transistors into smaller spaces, driving the continuous improvement in computing power.
• Cosmetics: nanoparticles of various materials are used in moisturisers, foundations and anti-ageing creams to improve texture and penetration.

Key Fact

Nanoparticles are used in sunscreens (UV absorption), wound dressings (antibacterial silver nanoparticles), self-cleaning glass (photocatalysis), drug delivery (targeted medicine) and electronics (smaller transistors).

Risks and Scientific Uncertainty

Nanoparticles present genuine unknowns that make risk assessment difficult. Because they are small enough to cross cell membranes, enter the bloodstream through the lungs, and potentially accumulate in organs, they may cause harm in ways that larger particles of the same material would not. Research into their long-term effects on human health and the environment is still developing.

When scientific data is limited, decision-makers face a dilemma. Banning a technology prematurely prevents potential benefits (better medicines, more effective sun protection) and may push users towards alternatives that have their own risks. Allowing a technology without adequate testing could expose large numbers of people to harm that only becomes apparent later. Reasonable people can disagree on the right course of action when evidence is uncertain — this is not a failure of science but a feature of how new technologies develop.

Scientists and regulators distinguish between hazard (the potential to cause harm) and risk (the probability of harm occurring in real-world conditions). A substance may be hazardous in laboratory conditions but pose low risk in normal use if exposure is minimal or the substance is effectively contained. Good risk-benefit reasoning always asks: compared with what? If the alternative to nano-titanium-dioxide sunscreen is no sun protection at all, the risk calculus changes.

Environmental concerns are also relevant. Nanoparticles washed off skin or released from products can enter waterways. Silver nanoparticles, for instance, are toxic to aquatic organisms at the concentrations released by some products. Whether this constitutes a significant ecological risk depends on toxicity levels and dilution in real water bodies — an ongoing area of research.

From an exam perspective, the key skill is to evaluate a named scenario using evidence: identify the benefit clearly, identify the risk clearly, acknowledge what is unknown, and reach a justified conclusion about whether the use is appropriate. Questions in this area are almost always levels-marked and reward reasoning over lists of facts.

glossary_terms.definition: A particle with dimensions in the range 1–100 nanometres (nm), where 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m.
The ratio of a particle’s exposed surface area to its total volume; smaller particles have a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio.
A form of carbon made of a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice; it is extremely strong and conducts electricity well.
The process of weighing the potential harms of an action or technology against its likely benefits, particularly when scientific evidence is incomplete.
Nanoparticles made of silver which kill bacteria by releasing silver ions that disrupt bacterial cell membranes.
The concentration of a substance that is lethal to 50% of a test population under specified conditions, used to compare toxicity.

before.content_html:
Why Do We Need Chemical Analysis?

Chemists often need to identify unknown substances. This might be to check whether a water supply is safe, to identify minerals in rocks, to verify the purity of a manufactured product, or to analyse an unknown sample in a forensic investigation. The tools available fall into two broad categories: traditional chemical tests that rely on visible observations, and modern instrumental methods that use machines for faster, more accurate results. This lesson covers the tests you need to know and how to apply them systematically.

Flame Tests

A flame test identifies metal ions by the colour they produce when heated in a Bunsen burner flame. Different metal ions emit light of different colours because their electrons absorb energy and then release it as visible light at characteristic wavelengths. To carry out a flame test: dip a clean nichrome wire loop in concentrated hydrochloric acid (to remove previous residues), then dip it into the sample, and hold it in a blue Bunsen flame. The wire must be cleaned thoroughly between tests to avoid contamination, which would give misleading results.

Key Fact

Flame test colours: Lithium — crimson red. Sodium — yellow. Potassium — lilac. Calcium — orange-red. Copper — green / blue-green.

Tests for Gases

Four common gases have reliable, distinctive tests that you must know:

• Hydrogen (\ (H_2\)): hold a burning splint near the mouth of the test tube — a squeaky pop confirms hydrogen igniting with oxygen in the air.
• Oxygen (\ (O_2\)): insert a glowing splint into the gas — it relights because oxygen supports combustion.
• Carbon dioxide (\ (CO_2\)): bubble the gas through limewater — it turns milky or cloudy because calcium carbonate precipitates: \(Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O\).
• Chlorine (\ (Cl_2\)): hold damp litmus paper near the gas — it first turns red (chlorine is acidic) then is bleached white.

Testing for Metal Ions with Sodium Hydroxide

Adding sodium hydroxide solution (NaOH) to a solution containing metal ions produces coloured precipitates. The precipitate forms because metal ions react with hydroxide ions to produce an insoluble metal hydroxide. The colour of the precipitate identifies the metal ion present.

Calcium ions (\(Ca^{2+}\)) — white precipitate of calcium hydroxide.
Copper(II) ions (\(Cu^{2+}\)) — blue precipitate of copper hydroxide.
Iron(II) ions (\(Fe^{2+}\)) — green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide.
Iron(III) ions (\(Fe^{3+}\)) — brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide.
Aluminium ions (\(Al^{3+}\)) — white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH (aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric).
Magnesium ions (\(Mg^{2+}\)) — white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess NaOH.
The distinction between aluminium and magnesium is frequently tested: both produce white precipitates, but only aluminium’s dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide.

Testing for Negative Ions (Anions)

Several anions can be identified using specific reagents:

• Carbonate ions (\(CO_3^{2-}\)): add dilute acid. Carbon dioxide gas is produced and turns limewater milky.
• Sulfate ions (\(SO_4^{2-}\)): acidify with dilute hydrochloric acid first, then add barium chloride solution. A white precipitate of barium sulfate (\(BaSO_4\)) confirms sulfate ions.
• Halide ions: acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add silver nitrate solution. Chloride ions (\(Cl^-\)) give a white precipitate of silver chloride; bromide ions (\(Br^-\)) give a cream precipitate of silver bromide; iodide ions (\(I^-\)) give a yellow precipitate of silver iodide.

Key Fact

Halide tests with silver nitrate (after acidifying with dilute nitric acid): chloride → white precipitate. Bromide → cream precipitate. Iodide → yellow precipitate. Always acidify first to prevent interference from carbonate or sulfate ions.

Separation and Purity

Analysis often begins with separating a mixture into its components. The technique used depends on the physical properties of the substances involved:

• Filtration — separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The mixture is poured through filter paper; the solid (residue) stays on the paper and the liquid (filtrate) passes through.
• Distillation — separates a liquid from a dissolved solid by heating the solution. The liquid evaporates, is cooled in a condenser, and collected as a pure distillate. A mixture of liquids with different boiling points can be separated by fractional distillation.
• Chromatography — separates a mixture of dissolved substances by how strongly each component is attracted to the stationary phase (paper) versus how soluble it is in the mobile phase (solvent).

Each spot on a chromatogram has an Rf value that can be used to identify it.

$$R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by substance}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}$$

Example: The solvent front travels 12.0 cm. A pigment spot travels 9.0 cm.
\(R_f = \frac{9.0}{12.0} = 0.75\)
Rf values are always between 0 and 1. A pure substance produces a single spot with a consistent Rf value under the same conditions. A mixture produces multiple spots.

A pure substance melts and boils at fixed, sharp temperatures. Impurities lower the melting point and broaden the melting range. Checking a substance’s melting point against a known value is therefore a simple way to test purity in the laboratory.

Instrumental Methods

Instrumental methods of analysis are faster, more sensitive and more accurate than traditional chemical tests. Gas chromatography separates the components of a mixture by passing it through a column in which each component travels at a different rate, producing separate peaks. The number of peaks tells you how many components are in the mixture, and the retention time identifies each substance. Mass spectrometry gives the relative molecular mass of a substance by measuring the mass-to-charge ratio of its ions. Gas chromatography linked with mass spectrometry (GC-MS) is particularly powerful because it both separates and identifies components in a single analysis.

Work systematically. First dissolve the sample in water. Use a flame test to suggest the cation (positive ion). Confirm the cation by adding sodium hydroxide and observing the precipitate colour. Then test for the anion: silver nitrate for halides, barium chloride for sulfates, dilute acid for carbonates. Record all observations carefully and compare with known reference data. If chemical tests are inconclusive, instrumental methods such as GC-MS can identify substances with greater certainty.
